query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single-step hybrid processing intervention combining cryogenic rolling with subsequent warm annealing (using specific parameter windows) can refine the lamellar colony into a hierarchical, dual-scale microstructure that simultaneously boosts strength and ductility in eutectic HEAs.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic HEA with coarse-scale, as-cast dual-phase lamellar colonies that are prone to early microcracking due to limited strain partitioning.
generation.intervention: Implement a hybrid processing route: first, perform cryogenic rolling with a reduction of approximately 50–70% at liquid-nitrogen temperatures to introduce high dislocation density; then apply a controlled warm annealing at around 450°C for about 10 minutes to trigger partial recrystallization and generate microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.conditions: The processing must use cryogenic deformation at 50–70% reduction followed immediately by warm annealing at ~450°C for ~10 minutes, ensuring partial recovery without full recrystallization or phase instability.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchical microstructure featuring ultrafine recrystallized grains intermixed with retained larger lamellar regions, which creates strain gradients and robust phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The high-density dislocations and stored strain energy produced by cryogenic rolling enable localized partial recrystallization during warm annealing. This in turn creates a dual-scale microstructure that promotes load partitioning and increases back-stress hardening, delaying crack initiation and propagation while simultaneously raising both yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the hybrid-processed alloy is expected to exhibit a marked increase in yield strength (potentially approaching ultrahigh strength levels) and a significant improvement in ductility (as evidenced by higher uniform elongation and delayed crack propagation), with experimental property gains being sensitive to the chosen parameters.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic HEA presenting uniform, coarse lamellar colonies susceptible to early microcrack coalescence under tensile loading.
generation.boundary: The approach is effective only if the processing parameters remain within the prescribed windows; excessive deformation or overly high annealing temperatures could lead to complete recrystallization or unwanted phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of property improvements is uncertain and will depend on fine tuning of cryogenic reduction and annealing parameters. Nonetheless, prior work supports that hierarchical microstructures enhance both strength and ductility.

falsification_experiment.design: Process a set of eutectic HEA samples by subjecting them to cryogenic rolling (50–70% reduction) followed by warm annealing at 450°C for 10 minutes. Prepare a control group of as-cast samples. Characterize the microstructure using EBSD and TEM, then conduct standardized room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Grain size distribution and microstructural heterogeneity via EBSD/TEM
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation from tensile tests
Fracture surface analysis to assess crack initiation and propagation patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid-processed samples do not show a clear hierarchical microstructure and if their tensile properties (strength and ductility) are not statistically improved relative to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. Producing in situ composite materials with superior strength and ductility has long been a challenge. Here, the authors use lamellar microstructure inherited from casting, rol

Unlike microstructural heterogeneities, which have been investigated so far to achieve strength-ductility synergy in different materials,, including HEAs,,, the novel strategy developed in the present research leads to a different paradigm featured by dual structural-compositional heterogeneities. On the microstructural side, the heterogeneities are ensured by the presence of the LRs and NCRs, while on the compositional side it is featured by a number of different constituents. While the LRs consist of L12 and B2 (containing disordered nano-precipitates), the NCRs contain different ordered and disordered phases with differences in structure, composition and internal strain or defect densities. Evidently, the dual structural-compositional heterogeneities offer a large number of interfaces and boundaries separating widely different hardness domains and phases. The massive back-stress strengthening in such heterogeneous microstructural arrangements results in super-strong EHEA coupled with appreciable ductility. It is interesting to note that monotonic cryo-rolling and novel variants such as hybrid-rolling (cryo- followed by warm-rolling) have been exploited by us in our earlier research to achieve novel structural and/or compositionally heterogeneous microstructure in multiphase lamellar eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA. The vastly different hardness of the constituent phases results in differential strain-partitioning, which in turn, results in differential stored energy or driving force for recrystallization during annealing and warm-rolling. In contrast, in the present research, the same cryo-rolling is exploited to tune the heterogeneous precipitation behavior for achieving the heterogeneous microstructure. These results clearly indicate significant opportunities for achieving novel heterogeneous microstructures in a wide range of HEAs through innovative processing by cryo-rolling.
